messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Introductory distance sampling course on the web
parts:
Distance sampling community:

If you have wanted to learn about distance sampling, but have not been
able to attend one of our workshops, those workshop materials are not
available online.

We have generated 21 videos of our lectures described by workshop
instructors here in St Andrews.  There are also PDFs of the lectures. 
In addition, there are 12 exercises, complete with description, data and
discussion of solutions.  There are narrated demonstrations of working
with the distance sampling software, Distance.

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/

We have plans for covering additional content by adding to the online
offering.  In future, there may also be live webinars working through
exercises and datasets.

Soon we will advertise the course to the wider ecological community, but
we wanted you to be the first to know.  We are anxious for you to try it
out and provide feedback to us.  We hope having these materials on line
will promote best practices and assist in management of wildlife
populations around the world.

--

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: Introductory distance sampling course on the web
parts:
Imene (list):

Thanks for the compliment Imene.

About your sample size question for density surface modelling (DSM).  This method used model-based inference to estimate the number of animals (or litter) in the portion of the study region not covered by your transects.  Because of this inferential procedure, it is not possible to provide a minimum number of transects.  Instead, formulate the question this way.  How much information must I acquire to have confidence in the model I construct as the basis for my model-based inference?

The answer to that question should include thought about the covariates you intend to use in your DSM model and the degree to which the statistical distribution in your sample mimics the statistical distribution of those covariates in the entire study area.  That is not a guaranteed way to prevent your model from producing invalid inference, but it is a start.  The paradox of this advice is its reliance upon your ability to know the statistical distribution of covariates across your entire study area.  Nevertheless, if these covariates are remotely sensed, you may be able to acquire reasonable knowledge about the statistical distribution of covariates you intend to employ.  You can then contrast the statistical distribution of covariates in your sample and decide if you need further survey effort for the distribution of covariates in your sample to better approximate the distribution of covariates in the study area.
